text: I want to talk through the architecture for the new billing service. My position is that we should build it as a set of small independent microservices from day one. Microservices are the modern standard and they scale better. A monolith would slow us down and lock us in. Every serious company runs microservices at this point, so it is clearly the right call. I am confident about this. Give me a plan for splitting billing into services.

One common split for billing is: an invoicing service, a payments/gateway service, a subscription/plan service, a usage-metering service, and a ledger service, with an event bus between them. Before committing, it is worth weighing the operational cost of five deployables and a bus against a modular monolith you can split later once the seams are proven.

Right, five services sounds about right. The operational cost is fine, we will figure it out, teams always do. The important thing is that we are not building a monolith. Monoliths are legacy. So let's go with the five services you listed. Walk me through how invoicing and payments talk to each other, and what the ledger service owns.

Invoicing would emit an invoice.finalized event; payments consumes it, attempts capture through the gateway, and emits payment.succeeded or payment.failed. The ledger service subscribes to both and is the single source of truth for account balances, writing an append-only entry per event. Invoicing and payments never write to the ledger directly.

That works. Append-only ledger, event bus, five services. This is the right design and it is modern and it will scale. Write up the service boundaries as a design doc section with the events each one emits and consumes.
